page.overview:
Who is Abdul ben Raschid?

Abdul ben Raschid ben Moussad, ben Osman known as the Great Sheikh of Lost Bel Aliad, Son of the Shifting Sands, and Lord of the Malaluk Desert, was an Arabyan prince many millenia ago.

He alone beheld what no other mortal had for millennia before even the birth of the demigod Sigmar. Driven by the cruel passion of his curiosity and the pitiless momentum of destiny, Abdul hen Raschid wandered the lands of ancient Nehekhara for eight long years, recording all he saw within the masterpiece that he could not bring himself to name, but which history has named the Book of the Dead. It is to the few surviving copies of this great poem in blank verse that the scholars of the Old World owe their hazy knowledge of ancient Nehekhara.

As is often the way of such things, hen Raschid did not live to see the widespread horror inspired by his work. Whether it was because he sought to emulate some of the dangerous arts he beheld during his travels, or whether he was cursed simply by witnessing all he had, the prince died under mysterious circumstances, strangled while locked within a shuttered room. When his servants eventually broke down the door, they found only his purple-faced corpse. His body was said to have been so chilling to the touch that it burned the hands of those who tried to lift it.

Terrified by these events and ignorant of the great value of ben Raschid's work, the Caliph of the eastern city of Ka-Sabar ordered all copies of the prince's book to be found and burned. Fortunately for history and seekers of wisdom, the Caliph was not entirely successful in his destructive efforts. Copies survived in the private collections of nobles who were unaware of the identity or worth of the book they owned. In time, the zealous knights of the Empire, Tilea, and Bretonnia declared their crusade against the lands of Araby, and among the spoils they brought back from their campaign were copies of the Book of the Dead.
